# Judith Chapter 2 — Disagreement Log
**Arbiter:** SOPHIA | **In council with:** EMET, LOGOS, PNEUMA
**Date:** 2026-03-17

---

## Summary
Total disagreements: 16

---

## Disagreement 1 — Verse 2:1: "a word went forth" vs. "a decree"

**EMET:** "there-was a word in-the house of Nebuchadnezzar" — literal rendering of λόγος ἐγενήθη.
**LOGOS:** "a decree went forth from the house of Nebuchadnezzar."
**PNEUMA:** "Nebuchadnezzar made his move" — paraphrases entirely.
**SOPHIA ruling:** LOGOS. "Decree" appropriately captures the royal/official register of λόγος in this context. EMET's "word" is technically accurate but ambiguous. PNEUMA's paraphrase loses the formal announcement entirely.

---

## Disagreement 2 — Verse 2:2: "secret counsel" (βουλὴν αὐτοῦ)

**EMET:** "his secret counsel."
**LOGOS:** "his secret plan."
**PNEUMA:** "his plan."
**SOPHIA ruling:** LOGOS. "Secret plan" captures both the Greek βουλή (plan/counsel) and the deliberate concealment implied by the council setting. PNEUMA loses the secrecy element.

---

## Disagreement 3 — Verse 2:3: "had not obeyed the word of his mouth"

**EMET:** "who-had-not-obeyed the-word of-his mouth."
**LOGOS:** "who had not obeyed the word of his mouth."
**PNEUMA:** "who had ignored his command."
**SOPHIA ruling:** LOGOS. Preserves the biblical idiom "word of his mouth" (ῥῆμα τοῦ στόματος αὐτοῦ) which echoes royal decree language throughout the book.

---

## Disagreement 4 — Verse 2:4: "second after him" vs. "second only to himself"

**EMET:** "the-second [man] after him."
**LOGOS:** "who was second only to himself."
**PNEUMA:** "the second most powerful man in the empire."
**SOPHIA ruling:** LOGOS. "Second only to himself" is natural English for the Greek δεύτερος ἀπ' αὐτοῦ. PNEUMA's "in the empire" adds an interpretive gloss.

---

## Disagreement 5 — Verse 2:5: Speech introduction

**EMET:** "Thus says the-great king, the-lord of all-the earth."
**LOGOS:** "Thus says the great king, the lord of all the earth."
**PNEUMA:** "This is the decree of the great king, lord of all the earth."
**SOPHIA ruling:** LOGOS/EMET. The formula τάδε λέγει is a prophetic/royal messenger formula ("Thus says") — it should be preserved for its rhetorical weight and biblical resonance. PNEUMA's "decree" front-loads a formality the Greek does not use here.

---

## Disagreement 6 — Verse 2:5: "men who trust in their own strength"

**EMET:** "men who-trust in their-own strength."
**LOGOS:** "men confident in their own strength."
**PNEUMA:** "veterans, men who trust their own strength."
**SOPHIA ruling:** LOGOS. "Confident in their own strength" is natural and accurate. PNEUMA adds "veterans" without Greek warrant.

---

## Disagreement 7 — Verse 2:7: "earth and water" (γῆν καὶ ὕδωρ)

**EMET/LOGOS/PNEUMA:** All preserve "earth and water."
**PNEUMA:** Adds "as tokens of submission" as an explanatory gloss.
**SOPHIA ruling:** The phrase "earth and water" is preserved unglossed. The cultural practice (Herodotean submission formula) is well known; a footnote is appropriate but the gloss in the text breaks narrative flow.

---

## Disagreement 8 — Verse 2:7: "give them over as plunder" vs. "hand them over"

**EMET:** "I-will-give them as-plunder to them."
**LOGOS:** "hand them over as plunder."
**PNEUMA:** "I will hand everything over to be plundered."
**SOPHIA ruling:** LOGOS. The Greek δώσω αὐτοὺς εἰς διαρπαγήν = "I will give them to plunder/pillage." LOGOS's "give them over as plunder" preserves this. PNEUMA's "everything" broadens the referent.

---

## Disagreement 9 — Verse 2:8: Death imagery

**EMET:** "their slain-ones will-fill their ravines... the river will-be-filled with their dead... every-overflow and valley of-the mountains will-be-filled with the-cast-out of-their flesh."
**LOGOS:** "Their slain shall fill every ravine and gully; the river will be choked with their dead; and every overflowing stream and mountain valley will be filled with the corpses of their flesh."
**PNEUMA:** "The dead will fill every ravine and wadi. The rivers will run with corpses. Every valley and mountain pass will be piled with their bodies."
**SOPHIA ruling:** LOGOS. "Gully" for χείμαρρος and "choked" for filling are vivid but accurate. PNEUMA's "wadi" is an anachronistic Middle Eastern term; "piled with their bodies" loses the specific image of cast-out flesh. "Corpses of their flesh" should be preserved as it reflects the rhetorical excess of the speech.

---

## Disagreement 10 — Verse 2:10: "guard them" vs. "hold them"

**EMET:** "guard them for-me until the-day of-their reproof."
**LOGOS:** "hold them for me until the day of their punishment."
**PNEUMA:** "keep them under guard for the day of reckoning."
**SOPHIA ruling:** LOGOS. "Until the day of their punishment" for εἰς ἡμέραν ἐλεγμοῦ αὐτῶν is accurate. "Reckoning" (PNEUMA) is acceptable but "punishment" is more precise to ἐλεγμός.

---

## Disagreement 11 — Verse 2:11: "let not your eye spare them"

**EMET:** "let-not your eye spare [them]."
**LOGOS:** "show no pity."
**PNEUMA:** "no mercy."
**SOPHIA ruling:** LOGOS. "Show no pity" is natural English that captures the sentiment. However, EMET's "let not your eye spare" — φεισάσθω ὁ ὀφθαλμός σου — is a distinctive idiom worth noting. LOGOS adopted for readability; EMET's literalism noted.

---

## Disagreement 12 — Verse 2:12: Oath formula

**EMET:** "by-my life and by-the power of my kingdom."
**LOGOS:** "as I live, and by the power of my kingdom."
**PNEUMA:** "by my life and my crown."
**SOPHIA ruling:** LOGOS. "As I live" is the standard English rendering of the Greek life-oath formula. PNEUMA's "crown" for βασιλεία (kingdom/reign) is too reductive.

---

## Disagreement 13 — Verse 2:15: "archers on horseback" vs. "mounted archers"

**EMET:** "twelve-thousand archers on-horseback."
**LOGOS:** "twelve thousand mounted archers."
**PNEUMA:** "twelve thousand cavalry."
**SOPHIA ruling:** LOGOS. "Mounted archers" is precise — the Greek specifies mounted bowmen (ἱππεῖς τοξότας), not simply cavalry. PNEUMA's "cavalry" is too general.

---

## Disagreement 14 — Verse 2:20: "like locusts and like the sand of the earth"

**EMET/LOGOS:** Preserve both similes.
**PNEUMA:** "as numberless as locusts, as the sand of the sea." (Changes "earth" to "sea.")
**SOPHIA ruling:** EMET/LOGOS. The Greek has τῆς γῆς (of the earth/land), not sea. Both similes preserved.

---

## Disagreement 15 — Verse 2:23: Plundering the desert peoples

**EMET:** "he-devastated Phud and Lud and plundered all-the sons of Rasses."
**LOGOS:** "He ravaged Phud and Lud, plundered all the Rassites."
**PNEUMA:** "He laid waste to Phud and Lud. He stripped the Rassites."
**SOPHIA ruling:** LOGOS. "Rassites" as a gentilized form of "sons of Rasses" is appropriate. PNEUMA's "stripped" loses the plundering sense of the Greek διήρπασεν.

---

## Disagreement 16 — Verse 2:28: Fear and trembling

**EMET:** "the-fear of him and the-trembling of him fell upon-the ones inhabiting the-seacoast."
**LOGOS:** "Fear of him and dread of him fell upon all who lived along the seacoast."
**PNEUMA:** "Panic ran ahead of him along the coast."
**SOPHIA ruling:** LOGOS. The Greek φόβος αὐτοῦ καὶ τρόμος αὐτοῦ is a formulaic double expression — "fear... and trembling/dread" — preserving both terms matters. PNEUMA's "panic ran ahead" is evocative but loses the formal idiom.
